content.body: > [!NOTE] > > Refer to https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/222202, packaging up Console for Cloud UI, for a real-world implementation of this Horizon. ## Introduction As our different web applications evolve and people begin to use them together, it becomes even more imperative that we share code. Today the EUI team does an amazing job building and maintaining a library of reusable, off-the-shelf components that adhere to the Elastic design language, enabling us to build consistent experiences. As we develop more patterns and use cases, it has become clear the EUI component library does not (and indeed, cannot) house all of the code our teams should share. We've had success in the past sharing Elastic-specific libraries through NPM, (e.g. [@elastic/charts](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@elastic/charts), [@elastic/ebt](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@elastic/ebt)) but as we've experienced, maintaining these libraries outside of our release cadence can be a challenge. We should explore ways to share code effectively between our web applications _without_ an independent NPM publish step. Indeed, the only function publishing to NPM provides is an OSS-safe storage and retrieval solution for Kibana that adds the ability for non-OSS applications to access the same code. ## Examples ### Proposed from Kibana today `TODO: clintandrewhall - get solid screenshots/examples of some items proposed thus far` ### From the POC > [!NOTE] > The proof-of-concept uses `@kbn/shared-ux-avatar-solution` and `@kbn/shared-ux-chrome-navigation` as test cases. ## General Approach Since Kibana is an open-source repository, and a majority of its code is organized into packages, we could devise a build process to build directories of code into packages for consumption internally, such as in the Cloud platform. ### Versioning - Since the code is static and publicly available, these assets would simply be archives of code at a particular SHA. - The version of the built package would be mapped to the released version of Kibana, (e.g. v8.18.1 or v9.0.1) and archived. - We would also maintain a `serverless` version, built with each serverless release. - We could consider a `canary` version, if the need were to arise. ### Storage The built assets would be hosted within an internal NPM instance. We could consider an internal repo in the interim. ### "Kibana-first" is _required_ The approach could be adopted by other applications wishing to share code. If that code needs to be consumed in _Kibana_, though, the source code and the build _must_ be moved to Kibana, (or published to NPM) As has been stated many times in many contexts: "Kibana is open source". The packages it consumes _must_ be publicly accessible. *This means shared code consumed by Kibana must originate in Kibana.* ## Proof-of-concept Implementation The following is a first-pass example of how this could work today. It regularly references the POC draft PR: https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/220847 ### 1. Identify and evaluate a package to share To share a package of code with another web application at Elastic, there are few caveats and considerations: #### Ensure the package is appropriate Components or utility logic are great for these kinds of shared code. Logic that requires an understanding or integration of Kibana fundamentals are unlikely to be successful, (or useful). Imagine we'd publish it to public NPM, and then take a look. #### Ensure the package to share is agnostic - Any dependencies on Kibana `core`, Kibana architecture, plugin lifecycle, state, etc will have to be accounted for in the consuming application. - Any `@kbn/*` dependency in the package will need to be declared as a peer dependency and _also_ built to be shared. - It could be bundled along with the package, but that should be avoided. - Any external dependency will also have to be present in the consuming application. - e.g. if your package uses `redux` to provide state, the consumer will need the same version, (and its dependencies) #### Aim low, or refactor - Try to find the lowest package in the chain, or one containing the bare minimum of code to accomplish the goal. - It's easier to refactor logic out into a simple, stateless package than deal with peer dependencies or stubbed context providers. ### 2. Prepare the package for build In the PoC, I adopted `webpack` as the build/bundling tool. I then created a `packaging` directory to house build assets: - `tsconfig.json` - `package.json` - `webpack.config.js` > [!NOTE] > I envisioned (and even started) a script to populate the `packaging` directory and even handle the builds. I paused that work to share the results thus far. All internal packages in Kibana have access to any of the dependencies in the `package.json`. That means any candidate for sharing will either 1/ bundle that dependency with the build, or 2/ need that dependency (in a compatible version) in the consuming application. #### `packaging/tsconfig.json` This `tsconfig.json` file is more or less unremarkable, and would likely be the same for any package. #### `packaging/package.json` This is a virtual copy of the package's `package.json` file, with the exception that the `version` field is set to the same version as the Kibana branch. Any dependencies that will be excluded from the build and expected to be in the consuming application need to be listed in the `peerDependencies` field: ```json { "name": "@kbn/shared-ux-avatar-solution", "version": "9.0.0", "license": "Elastic License 2.0 OR AGPL-3.0-only OR SSPL-1.0", "main": "index.js", "peerDependencies": { "@elastic/eui": "^9.0.0", "@emotion/react": "^11.0.0", "react": "^17" } } ``` #### `packaging/webpack.config.js` The `webpack.config.js` file is fairly standard, with one exception: any `peerDependencies` need to be listed in the `externals` property of the Webpack config: ```ts externals: { '@emotion/react': 'commonjs @emotion/react', '@emotion/styled': 'commonjs @emotion/styled', '@elastic/eui': 'commonjs @elastic/eui', react: 'commonjs react', }, ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > Any dependencies not listed both the `package.json` and `webpack.config.js` files will end up being bundled with the build. ### 3. Build the package In the POC, you can just invoke `webpack` and the code will be built into the `target` directory: ```bash npx webpack build --config ./src/path/to/package/packaging/webpack.config.js ``` For example, building `@kbn/shared-ux-avatar-solution`: ```bash npx webpack build --config ./src/platform/packages/shared/shared-ux/avatar/solution/packaging/webpack.config.js assets by status 68.4 KiB [cached] 1 asset asset index.js 25.1 KiB [compared for emit] (name: main) 1 related asset runtime modules 2.13 KiB 6 modules built modules 16.9 KiB (javascript) 68.4 KiB (asset) [built] cacheable modules 16.8 KiB (javascript) 68.4 KiB (asset) modules by path ../src/ 15.9 KiB (javascript) 68.4 KiB (asset) ../src/solution_avatar.tsx 15.9 KiB [built] [code generated] ../src/assets/texture.svg 68.4 KiB (asset) 42 bytes (javascript) [built] [code generated] ../index.tsx 530 bytes [built] [code generated] ../../../../../../../../node_modules/@babel/runtime/helpers/esm/extends.js 336 bytes [built] [code generated] external "@emotion/react" 42 bytes [built] [code generated] external "react" 42 bytes [built] [code generated] external "@elastic/eui" 42 bytes [built] [code generated] webpack 5.96.1 compiled successfully in 191 ms ``` > [!NOTE] > Notice that `@emotion/react`, `react`, and `@elastic/eui` were marked as externals and excluded from the output. Now we have built sources we can use in another application, like the Cloud platform. We just need to map to it in that application's `package.json`. > [!IMPORTANT] > The package also needs the `package.json` file and the `tsconfig.json` file. This would be handled by the CLI script I was starting to implement. ### 4. Map to that package (locally) Since we don't have a place to store the built assets in a reasonable way (yet), the easiest way to test this is to add an entry to the `target` directory in the local file system: ```json // package.json "@kbn/shared-ux-avatar-solution": "../path/to/kibana/package/target", "@kbn/shared-ux-chrome-navigation": "../path/to/kibana/package/target", ``` ### Results I started with two packages, one simple and one a bit more complex, (as well as realistic). #### Simple: Solution Avatar > A wrapper around `EuiAvatar` tailored for use in Kibana solutions. > > -- [`README`](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/main/src/platform/packages/shared/shared-ux/avatar/solution/README.mdx?plain=1) #### Realistic: Solution Navigation > Navigation container to render items for cross-app linking > > -- [README](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/main/src/platform/packages/shared/shared-ux/chrome/navigation/README.mdx?plain=1) ## Next steps and open questions I've spoken with @mistic at length on this topic, particularly around the build system we might use, (🎉 to him for his assistance with the POC!) ### Next steps ### Open questions

🌅 Note:   "Horizons" are R&D work that engineers regularly participate in.  They appear on the roadmap only to show that a variable portion of an engineer's time is devoted to this work.  There are no set deadlines or delivery dates for horizons.  Engineers are expected to "make progress" on the effort, which may span multiple months or even quarters.

## Background

The Kibana home page and plugin have traditionally served as the initial view for users upon starting or logging into Kibana. This page has been used to orient users, regardless of their experience level. However, for frequent users, the home page's usefulness diminishes due to its static nature and limited content management capabilities.

Although the concept of content management within the home page has been discussed over time, it has often been deprioritized. In serverless, solution-specific home pages with customized getting started experiences have replaced the general home page. However, even these solution home pages can become outdated.

## Horizon: Let's make Home feel more like a home.

A Horizon could aim to enhance the home plugin's utility by introducing and listing content relevant to the person and their role.  While proposing new content management metadata is possible, the focus should be on utilizing _existing_ data whenever possible, such as favorites, owned objects, recently accessed objects, and more. This approach would not only accelerate the inclusion of other useful objects on the home page but also encourage solutions and plugins to register their content with content management systems for home page visibility.

This Horizon presents an opportunity to make incremental and surgical improvements to the home page over time.

## Approach

> [!NOTE]
> Any code in this description is pseudo and has not been thoroughly considered.

1. Audit/confirm any existing object APIs and available metadata.
   - Created by
   - Tags
   - Favorites
   - Search
   - View counts (?)
   - others?
2. Audit confirm which objects support which of the above metadata fields.
   - For example, only dashboards use _created by_, _favorites_
3. Create shared component panels to render objects
4. Integrate panels into the Home plugin
   - V1 - Add recents, minimize focus on adding data
   - V2 - Add "tagged" objects
   - V3 - Add Favorites, Created By
5. Layout toggles?
   - The layout of the home page could flex based on what content a person has available, rather than asking them to customize it.
   - For example, if data has been ingested, we could move the ingest call-out up.
   - We could also automatically add a panel once they have a favorite, or a recent, etc.

## Open Questions

- Is there any other metadata or information that could be flexed into the home based on the viewer's experience with the platform?
- Could we, say, highlight AI Assistant or other "you've been here a while, what do you think of [xyz]".

## Design Reference

> [!NOTE]
> These designs are by no means final.  They are meant to inspire and guide exploration.

content.body:
🌅 Note:   "Horizons" are R&D work that engineers regularly participate in.  They appear on the roadmap only to show that a variable portion of an engineer's time is devoted to this work.  There are no set deadlines or delivery dates for horizons.  Engineers are expected to "make progress" on the effort, which may span multiple months or even quarters.

## Background

Notification Center is a common feature used by many websites and external tools.  Integrating a similar tool into Kibana has always made sense.

In 2020, we established requirements for a Notification Center that would use a service to enable any plugin to send, store, and federate notifications across Kibana instances. We also defined user experience requirements and commissioned EUI to create components for the Notification Center. Unfortunately, building the service layer and integrating the experience into Kibana was de-prioritized for more important projects, like Serverless, and has remained so.

## Horizon: Introduce a Notification Center UX, (and address an annoyance with it)

A Horizon could provide an opportunity to take an incremental step toward a Notification Center in Kibana, _and_ eliminate a known annoyance in the interface: redirecting toasts that either require manual dismissal and/or offer an action to a notification space.

For example, once a toast like "Your report is ready, do you want to view it?" is dismissed, it cannot be reviewed.  Redirecting the toast content to an event in the Notification Center would allow a person to review the content whenever they like.

## Approach

> [!NOTE]
> Code in this description is pseudo and has not been thoroughly considered.

We could model a new Events API on the Toasts API.  We could also reintroduce and refactor the notification event component that was written for and then removed from EUI.  Then we would display the notifications in a new space in the chrome.

1. Bring the EUI Notification Event component into Kibana.
2. Create a new API and services in `@kbn/core-notifications-browser` called `events`.
   - Create the API class.
   - Add methods for creating, marking as un/read, removing.
   - Add convenience method to "register" an event configuration.
3. Create a feature flag for `events`.  
   - if enabled, add the `event` to the list.
   - if disabled, route the `event` to a `toast` instead.
4. Add a Notification Center UX to the chrome.
   - in the existing chrome, add a button and use a flyout.
   - in the Workspace Chrome, create a new slice and tool.

### 1. Bring the EUI Notification Event component into Kibana

In 2021, EUI completed work on `EuiNotificationEvent` - https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/4531.  It was eventually [deprecated](https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/7122) and then [removed](https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/7434).

I have copied the components to Kibana and [committed them](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/commit/ba807d72d0d24e7200d8c4e46acd3ce44b1bd286) into a feature branch - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/217052

The `NotificationEvent` component has been copied over with minimal changes.  It offers _a lot_ of customization.  It was obviously designed to be as flexible as possible as Kibana added notifications to the platform.  For this effort (and moving forward), the customizable nature would actually pose a problem to consumers, and to Shared UX: creating them, maintaining consistency, etc.  We have a few options wrt how we handle the component:

1. We could significantly simplify the component, or
2. We could use a platform API to translate a request into a set of repeatable customizations.

At this point, I'm recommending Option 2.  I discuss this further in the next section.

### 2. Create a new API and services in `@kbn/core-notifications-browser` called `events`.

We can create a new API-- `events`-- based on the existing [`toasts`](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/main/src/core/packages/notifications/browser-internal/src/toasts/toasts_api.tsx#L52) API.  This would maintain consistency, perhaps even simplification in the future:

```ts
interface BaseNotificationEvent {
  id: string;
  timestamp: number;
  title: string;
  message: string;
  isRead: boolean;
  // etc
}

export interface NotificationEventTypeData {
  severity: string;
  badgeColor?: EuiBadgeProps['color'];
  iconType?: IconType;
  eventName: string;
  // etc 
}

export type NotificationEvent = BaseNotificationEvent & NotificationEventTypeData;
```

The service would have the same methods you'd expect: `get$`, `count$`, 'notify`, `markAsRead`, `remove`.  In addition, I would propose we add a convenience method: `registerType`.

#### Registering a configuration in advance: `registerType`

The `registerType` method would take `NotificationEventTypeData` and return a method to post a notification event.

- Plugins could register their type and use the resulting method in their application.
- Plugins could expose the method on their `start` contracts to make consistent notifications easier.
- Similar to `locators`, the service could allow for retrieving a registered type.
  - Core could register some types, for example.

These types could also be used to group similar notifications, (e.g. by `typeId`).

### 3. Create a feature flag for `events`.

All instances where we currently show a toast with a user action or a toast that needs to be manually dismissed would check a feature flag. If the flag is enabled, we would store the toast in the Events Service; if disabled, we would display it as a normal toast.

### 4. Add a Notification Center UX to the chrome.

We would integrate this into Kibana's header as a button and a flyout.  We could also add it to into the Workspace Chrome prototype as a tool while keeping the underlying service the same.

## References

- Notification Event Component
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/217052
  - https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/4531
  - https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/7122
  - https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/7434
- Relevant issues
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/49539
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/86251
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/102177
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/67270
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/53738
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/51547
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/140743
  - https://github.com/elastic/kibana-team/issues/276
  - https://github.com/elastic/cloud/issues/29365
- Documents
  - [UX Proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1A_sah--8h7Iy3__02ZaCW6Mh7CunGuTtIGT8-_24I-g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.4yt5mpt35xav)
  - [Notifications Center MVP](https://docs.google.com/document/d/14wqgAili4vEbaC-PyFS8_zIoH_6LcSnOEwJXr0L59W0/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.t1kdh8qzcd20)

content.body:
## Summary For any given illustration in Kibana, we maintain two discrete files: one for light mode, and one for dark mode. With the introduction of the Borealis theme, we would theoretically need to maintain _four_ versions of each illustration. ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fa31162b-f9fb-42ce-94ec-f9a53374a81b) By using CSS variables with appropriate fallbacks embedded in a single SVG, we can adapt the colors of the SVG to both the theme and color mode of Kibana. This will allow us to reduce the number of SVGs we need to maintain, and provide a more consistent UX between themes and color modes. This is a proof-of-concept which uses a single SVG file and a JSON file of tokens and their color values. These are both read by a React component-- `Illustration`-- which compiles the color profile and adds the SVG to the DOM. > [!TIP] > This approach is implemented in a POC: https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/206540 ## Approach - Define CSS variables for EUI theme colors, available globally on the `:root`. - Create a single SVG file - replace any `fill` attribute with a `style` attribute using a CSS variable and fallback HEX color. - Create a color profile JSON file - enumerate all variables and their color values. - define common, light, dark, as well as thematic common, light and dark colors. - if a variable uses a color from the EUI palette, use that variable. - use RGB subtraction to calculate color shifts in non-EUI colors. - Render the SVG. - render the SVG inline. - calculate styles to apply to the SVG based on the theme and color mode and values from the JSON file. - apply the CSS variables to the `:root` based on the theme and color mode, using `Global` from `@emotion/react`. ## Background Today, our illustrations are produced in two color modes: light and dark. The developer is responsible for shifting between the two images based on the color mode of Kibana. This means we must maintain two different images for each illustration. With the introduction of the Borealis theme, if we intend for our illustrations to change to the new color palette-- and related colors change with them-- we would now need to maintain _four_ different images for each illustration. Consider adding "developer blue", high-contrast, and print modes, and the number of images we need to maintain continues to multiply. ### SVG display options There are three options with which one can display an SVG in Kibana: #### 1. Image The SVG is imported as a path and provided to an image tag, or to CSS: ```tsx // Webpack returns the SVG as a path to the asset. import svg from './path/to/image.svg'; ``` > [!NOTE] > This is how most SVGs are consumed in Kibana today. This provides the least flexibility, as the SVG is treated as a static image. The developer much switch between light and dark modes manually. #### 2. React component The SVG is converted to a React component: ```tsx const SomeImage = () => ; return
; ``` This provides the most flexibility, as we can use `emotion` to flex the image based on the theme and color mode. Unfortunately, this means React has to maintain the entire SVG as a React tree. content.body:
# Summary

EUI provides core UI components to Kibana, Cloud UI, and other Elastic apps. We maintain a large set of components, many of which change frequently, and while we're pretty sure we can write performant code and have good processes to detect bugs early, there's always a risk of shipping something that could cause a performance downgrade.

Considering the scale of Kibana, any performance downgrade could result in unhappy customers, poor developer experience, and more. Some of our components are used thousands of times across the app, often rendered multiple times on a single page. Some of our components render once and only affect initial render times. Others re-render frequently, reacting to changing props - these may not be as expensive to render initially, but could significantly reduce the application's responsiveness when rendering new data, e.g., `EuiDataGrid`.

The goal of this horizon initiative is to implement a benchmarking framework that we can use to test the performance of EUI components, both when rendered in isolation as well as in Kibana and other real-world scenarios. Ideally, the solution would be flexible enough to allow testing the performance of any rendered element, not only EUI components.

# What exactly should we measure?

Measuring performance is _hard_. There are a ton of ways to approach it, and each comes with its advantages and disadvantages. What we care about is **measuring what a user would experience**.

What's important is that we should focus on measuring performance differences between versions (e.g., `main` and a pull request) instead of running a typical benchmark and aiming for the best score (time) possible. Time is very relative in this case and will massively differ between atom components like `EuiTitle` and ~organisms~ whales like `EuiDataGrid`. Each performance metric should be adjusted to fit the component it focuses on.

The purpose of this horizon is to propose and track flagging dynamic styles passed to `css` prop.

## Context

Emotion advises passing _truly_ dynamic styles to the `style` prop instead of the `css` prop ([source](https://emotion.sh/docs/best-practices#use-the-style-prop-for-dynamic-styles)).

> By dynamic styles, we mean styles that change frequently or are unique to a single element.

An example from Kibana: `src/platform/packages/private/kbn-grid-layout/grid/grid_section/grid_section_footer.tsx`

https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/c88328f2902564dfd283690ecfe9ed6384901837/src/platform/packages/private/kbn-grid-layout/grid/grid_section/grid_section_footer.tsx#L21-L56

For each section, a separate CSS will be generated (even with `useMemo`) causing a lot of duplication. The more sections are generated, the bigger duplication and CSS stylesheet, the likely less performant application.

Not saying this specific example is bad because I haven't ran the code. Just trying to portray a potentially dynamic style that we **may** want to put into `style` in line with the docs but in Kibana codebase.

Here is an example of a dynamic style (based on drag) applied directly to DOM instead of passed through `css` prop.

https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/9171743e8368a47503cf5892a8b7e47d35b42319/src/platform/packages/private/kbn-grid-layout/grid/grid_section/grid_section_drag_preview.tsx#L18-L50

## Problem

We want to help the developers spot these dynamic styles that are passed to `css` prop but should be redirected to the `style` prop or direct DOM manipulation. We want to do it runtime to provide guidance with high confidence. How do we flag dynamic styles that could _truly_ cause a performance issue? E.g. after 5th, 20th or 100th time that they are recalculated?

## Alternatives considered

- We considered adding ESLint rules but decided against it because a static code analysis tool cannot detect dynamic styles with 100% confidence.

## Options

1. Monkey patch `insert` function. We can do it through our `EuiProvider`, overriding `cache.insert` function. We can keep a map of styles and on having inserted the same style again, we can verify whether the saved value is the same as `serialized.styles`. If not, we can flag it as a dynamic style. [PoC](https://github.com/elastic/eui/pull/8797)
2. ...

## The way forward

- [ ] Different options are considered and added to the "Options" section
- [ ] PoC and / or documentation is created around each option's advantages, disadvantages, feasibility and limitations

> [!NOTE]
> Refer to the proof-of-concept PR for implementation details: #234343

## Introduction

As Kibana's test suite grows, so does the challenge of detecting unintended visual regressions across plugins and workflows. While we have robust functional tests via Scout, we currently lack a systematic way to capture and compare the *visual state* of Kibana at a given point in time.

This project explores adding Visual Regression Testing (VRT) infrastructure to Scout — enabling teams to capture immutable screenshots of Kibana at a particular SHA, and compare those snapshots against future runs to detect visual drift.

This work was originally developed as a PoC during **ON Week** and subsequently opened for review. Based on feedback from the Appex-QA team, it is now being continued as a dedicated Horizon project.

## What Was Built

The PoC ([#234343](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/234343)) introduces two new capabilities inside `@kbn/scout`:

### `visualRegression` Fixture

A new Playwright fixture that captures screenshots during test execution. Screenshots can be triggered in two ways:

- **Automatically, via `test.step`:** If a test uses `test.step`, a screenshot is taken at the end of each step. This is the preferred approach, as it minimizes disruptive changes across SHAs and provides a natural visual log of each workflow.
- **Manually, via the fixture:** Tests can call `visualRegression` directly to capture the full screen, a specific selector, or a named region at any point.

The fixture is gated behind a `SCOUT_VISUAL_REGRESSION_ENABLED` environment variable, so it has no impact on standard CI runs.

### VRT Reporter

A companion reporter collects all captured screenshots and writes them to the `.scout` output directory, organized by plugin. A `metadata.json` file is generated per plugin, providing structured output that can be consumed downstream — for hosting, comparison tooling, or archival.

As a side effect discovered during development: the step-by-step screenshots also serve as a powerful tool for *visually exploring and confirming workflows* in Kibana — a useful artifact beyond regression detection alone.

## Approach and Philosophy

The intent is not to run VRT on every PR or CI job. Instead, the expectation is that product and design teams establish a cadence for capture and confirmation — for example, prior to a major release, on a weekly schedule, or tied to a serverless release. The resulting assets can be stored anywhere and compared at any point.

> [!NOTE]
> The preference is to use `test.step` over direct fixture calls, to reduce structural churn in tests between SHAs.

## Feedback and Next Steps

After review by the Appex-QA team ([comment](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/234343#issuecomment-3411089676)), the recommended path forward is to house the VRT fixture, reporter, and runner changes in a **dedicated package** — separate from the core `@kbn/scout` package. This mirrors the approach taken with `@kbn/evals` ([#227453](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/227453)).

The rationale for this separation:
- Keeps the core Scout package focused and maintainable.
- Makes ownership clearer — the VRT package can evolve at its own pace.
- Enables a dedicated `visualTest` function to make test type explicit during discovery.
- Reduces the surface area of changes for teams adopting Scout without VRT needs.

Work continues as a new Horizon proposal, one that is separate from the Scout runtime.

# Kibana Visual Regression Testing v2

> [!NOTE]
> This is a continuation of https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/240452 using the learnings and feedback since the proof-of-concept was completed in Sep 2025.

## Overview

Kibana's UI surface area is constantly growing, and a reliable way to catch visual regressions is needed. Since Scout is already used to exercise UI behavior in CI, the goal of this proposal is to integrate Visual Regression Testing (VRT) directly into it.

Instead of bolting on an entirely separate toolchain, my aim is to make visual checkpoints a natural extension of Scout. This epic covers the foundational work proposed to get VRT running locally, establish baseline management in CI, and create a sane, sustainable PR review workflow.

## Core Principles

To ensure this system remains understandable and performant as adoption scales, I have anchored the proposed architecture to four rules:

  * **Scout is the Test Runner:** Functional and visual tests should live in the same ecosystem. VRT is an opt-in layer via the `visualTest` API, but the underlying engine remains Scout.
  * **Kibana Owns the Contract:** Kibana's runtime writes the versioned manifests and artifacts. Future review tools (like Driftik) will adapt to Kibana's output, not the other way around.
  * **CI Owns Baseline Lineage:** Local runtimes capture screenshots, but the logic for deciding canonical hashes or branch comparisons belongs strictly to Buildkite and remote storage.
  * **PR Attribution is Separate from Release Drift:** To make PR reviews actionable, PRs are compared only against published `main` baselines. I plan to tackle release-level drift (comparing `main` to the last serverless release) as a separate future problem.

## Execution Strategy: The PR Stack

I am proposing to roll this out in heavily focused, review-sized PRs to establish clear operational boundaries:

  * https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/258987
This establishes the authoring model. Kibana learns to author checkpoints in Scout, capture images, and write stable local artifacts and manifests.
  * https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/258991
This introduces CI baseline generation. It allows CI to generate and publish canonical `main` baselines to remote storage as both expanded directories and highly portable `tar.gz` archives.
  * https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/258992
This closes the loop for reviewers. Labeled PRs (`ci:vrt`) will pull the latest `main` baseline, run a comparison, and publish a temporary HTML review site to highlight visual diffs.

## Architecture & Storage at a Glance

Run artifacts and baselines are strictly separated to keep CI and downstream tooling workflows clean:

  * **Run Artifacts:** Stored under `.scout/test-artifacts/vrt/...`.
  * **Local Baselines:** Kept outside the artifact tree under `.scout/baselines/vrt/...`.
  * **Canonical `main` Baselines:** Written to `gs://ci-artifacts.kibana.dev/vrt/baselines/...` via an `index.json` catalog.
  * **Bundle Partitioning:** Remote baselines are partitioned by location, architecture, domain, browser, and viewport.

## Next Steps: Driftik & Release Drift

While PR3 provides a temporary static HTML report to prove the data flow works, it is not the final proposed UI.

  * **PR4 (Driftik Integration):** I propose swapping the temporary HTML site for Driftik. Kibana will publish a Driftik-compatible adapter manifest alongside a pinned Driftik static bundle to serve as the long-term review UI.
  * **Release-Drift Reporting:** Following the Driftik integration, the next step is to build a cumulative report comparing the latest `main` baseline against the last serverless release to gauge overall release confidence.

## Demo Strategy

Before merging to `main`, I will validate the stack by demonstrating the end-to-end flow:

1.  Show local capture mode, baseline generation, and compare mode.
2.  Seed a remote baseline using the PR2 publisher.
3.  Open a labeled PR (using PR3 logic) to demonstrate hydration, comparison, and the review site.
4.  Run three test scenarios: a clean compare, an intentional visual change, and a missing-baseline failure.
content.title: [horizon] Visual Regression Testing v2

## Summary

I've been exploring a "designer toolbar" prototype that adds an in-page commenting and annotation layer to Kibana — a way for designers, PMs, and reviewers to leave contextual feedback on specific UI elements without leaving the product. It tries to replicate what was done for the developer toolbar. With the recent #268744 landing significant design tooling inside the developer toolbar (`@kbn/design-tools`), I want to surface this work now and open a conversation about where this kind of capability should live.

See short demo:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d988c87f-01ed-4dca-830e-78f9a635dca5

## What I've been prototyping

Working in a branch, I've been exploring:

- A new toolbar called designer toolbar
- Inline annotations anchored to specific elements on the page (works with flyouts, etc).
- A floating UI in the bottom right corner of the page that shows the lists of comment on a page (even if they're not visible, for example if a flyout is closed).
- A model where reviewers can leave feedback in shared environments (not just dev) via kibana.yml. Note: In my PoC annotations are saved as a saved object but I don't know how acceptable that would be. 

It's early. I have a working shell but I haven't landed on persistence and other implementation details. I need engineering help to take it further.

## Why I'm raising this now

PR #268744 (`@kbn/design-tools`) adds an interactive DOM editor — drag, resize, edit, undo/redo, live EUI components — overlaid on Kibana pages. It's a powerful tool for prototyping and tweaking UI in-place.

This is great, but it surfaces a question worth asking explicitly before the boundary gets set by default: as the developer toolbar accumulates more design-adjacent functionality, **do the tools in #268744 belong in the developer toolbar, or in a dedicated designer toolbar?**

## What I'm asking for

- **Feedback on the question above.** Can we have a designer toolbar? would be move the design-tools to the designer toolbar?
- **An engineering partner.** I have design + prototype work, but I need help thinking through architecture, persistence, and what it would take to ship this. @kowalczyk-krzysztof — you have the most relevant recent context; I'd love your perspective.
- **Visibility for the @elastic/appex-sharedux team.** I want this thinking to happen with input from the team that owns this space, rather than in parallel.

## Status

- Designer prototype: in progress (branch link TODO)
- Engineering implementation: not started
- Open questions: where it lives, how it persists, who it's for, what shipping looks like
